profile.reading:
This Lumen colocation facility, internally identified in public records as Sunnyvale 1, is located at 1380 Kifer Road, Sunnyvale, CA 94086; Lumen does not publish individual building addresses or specs on its own site for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink (renamed Lumen on September 14, 2020, with its stock ticker changing from CTL to LUMN on September 18, 2020) and built in part on CenturyLink's November 1, 2017 acquisition of Level 3 Communications, operates this facility as part of a network-centric edge colocation product rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen's own colocation data sheet states more than 175 carrier-neutral data centers across more than 60 North American markets, offering cabinet power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range described as varying by site; unlike the wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, Lumen does not disclose per-building square footage or total MW capacity for any of its sites.

California regulators are actively reworking how large data center loads are billed and interconnected as demand grows statewide, directly relevant to the dense Sunnyvale/Silicon Valley colocation submarket. Under SB 57 (2025), the California Public Utilities Commission opened a rate-design rulemaking in April 2026 addressing electric rate impacts of data centers and other large transmission-connected loads, expected to run roughly two years and examine dedicated data-center tariffs and the risk of costs shifting onto residential and small-business ratepayers. The California Independent System Operator separately published a formal issue paper on large-load interconnection considerations in January 2026.

Sunnyvale sits within the dense Silicon Valley colocation and carrier-hotel corridor that has drawn network-edge providers like Lumen alongside larger wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, a submarket shaped as much by fiber interconnection density as by raw power availability.

reading.body:
Lumen Sunnyvale 1 is a carrier-neutral colocation facility in the dense Silicon Valley fiber corridor, but Lumen does not publish power capacity, floor area, or rack count for any of its 175-plus North American sites. The company's own data sheet specifies cabinet-level power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range by location, which is consistent with network-edge colocation rather than hyperscale AI training density. Without published specifications this facility cannot be ranked within California's AI infrastructure or assessed for relevance to large-scale compute deployment.

California's regulatory environment is in active flux around data center interconnection and rates. The Public Utilities Commission opened a rulemaking in April 2026 expected to run roughly two years on electric rate design for data centers and other large transmission-connected loads, and the state's grid operator published a formal issue paper on large-load interconnection in January 2026. These proceedings will reshape how new power demand in Sunnyvale and Silicon Valley is billed and connected, creating material uncertainty for operators planning new capacity.

Sunnyvale sits within one of the nation's densest carrier-hotel submarkets, shaped by fiber density and network interconnection rather than raw power availability. This geography suits edge colocation and distributed network services far more than consolidated hyperscale campuses. The facility matters to AI infrastructure only if its location in this fiber corridor and Lumen's network reach make it useful as an edge point within a larger distributed architecture, a role for which no tenant or application data is published.
